source_text: Sic et paenitentiam apud illum praue interpretaris, quasi proinde mobilitate uel improuidentia, immo iam ex delicti recordatione paeniteat, quoniam quidem dixerit: paenituit, quod regem fecerim Saul, praescribens scilicet paenitentiam confessionem sapere mali operis alicuius uel erroris. porro non semper. euenit enim (et) in bonis factis paenitentiae confessio, ad inuidiam et exprobrationem eius. qui beneficii ingratus extiterit. sicut et tunc circa personam Saulis onerandam adnuntiatur a creatore, qui non deliquerat, cum Saulem adsumit in regnum et sancto spiritu auget; optimum enim adhuc qualis, inquit, non erat in filiis Israhelis — dignissime adlegerat. sed nec ignorauerat ita euenturum. nemo enim te sustinebit improuidentiam adscribentem deo ei, quem deum non negans confiteris et prouidum. haec enim illi propria diuinitas constat. sed malum factum Saulis, ut dixi, onerabat paenitentiae suae professione, quam uacante delicto circa Saulis adlectionem consequens est inuidiosam potius intellegi, non criminosam. ecce, inquis, criminosam eam animaduerto circa Niniuitas, dicente scriptura Ionae: et paenituit dominum de malitia, quam dixerat facturum se illis, nec fecit. sicut et ipse Ionas ad deum: propterea praeueni profugere in Tharsos, quia cognoueram te esse misericordem et miserescentem. patientem et plurimum misericordiae, paenitentem malitiarum. bene igitur, quod praemisit optimi dei titulum, patientissimi scilicet super malos et abundantissimi misericordiae et miserationis super agnoscentes et deplangentes delicta sua, quales tunc Niniuitae, si enim optimus qui talis, de isto prius cessisse debebis, non competere in talem, id est in optimum, etiam malitiae concursum. et quia et Marcion defendit arborem bonam malos; quoque fructus non licere producere, sed malitiam tamen nominauit ***, quod optimus non capit, numquid aliqua interpretatio subest earum malitiarum intellegendarum, quae possint et in optimum decucurrisse? subest autem. dicimus denique malitiam nunc significari non quae ad naturam redigatur creatoris, quasi mali, sed quae ad potestatem, quasi iudicis; secundum quam enuntiarit: ego sum qui condo mala, et: ecce ego emitto in uos mala, non peccatoria, sed ultoria. quorum satis diluimus infamiam ut congruentium iudici. sicut autem, licet mala dicantur, non reprehenduntur in iudice nec hoc nomine suo malum iudicem ostendunt, ita et malitia haec erit intellegenda nunc, quae ex illis malis iudiciariis deputata cum ipsis competat iudici. nam et apud Graecos interdum malitiae pro uexationibus et laesuris, non pro malignitatibus* ponuntur, sicut et in isto articulo. atque adeo si eius malitiae paenituit creatorem quasi creaturam, reprobandae scilicet et delictum iudicandae, atquin nec hic ullum admissum criminosum reputabitur creatori, qui iniquissimam ciuitatem digne meritoque decreuerat abolendam. ita quod iuste destinauerat. non male destinans, ex iustitia, non ex malitia destinarat: sed poenam ipsam malitiam nominauit ex malo et merito passionis ipsius. ergo. dices. si malitiam iustitiae nomine excusas, quia iuste exitium destinarat in Niniuitas, sic quoque culpandus est, qui iustitiae utique non paenitendae paenitentiam gessit. immo nec iustitiae, inquam, paenitebit deum, et superest iam agnoscere, quid sit paenitentia dei. non enim, si hominem ex recordatione plurimum delicti, interdum et ex alicuius boni operis ingratia paenitet, ideo et deum proinde. in quantum enim deus nec malum admittit nec bonum damnat, in tantum nec paenitentiae boni aut mali apud eum locus est. nam et hoc tibi eadem scriptura determinat, dicente Samuhele Sauli: discidit dominus regnum Israhelis de manu tua hodie et dabit illud proximo tuo, optimo super te, et scindetur Israhel in duas partes, et non conuertetur neque paenitentiam aget, quia non sicut homo est ad paenitendum, haec itaque definitio in omnibus aliam formam diuinae paenitentiae statuit, quae neque ex improuidentia neque ex leuitate neque ex ulla boni aut mali operis damnatione reputetur, sicut humana. quis ergo erit mos paenitentiae diuinae? iam relucet, si non ad humanas condiciones eam referas. nihil enim aliud intellegetur quam simplex conuersio sententiae prioris, quae etiam sine reprehensione eius possit admitti, etiam in homine, nedum in deo, cuius omnis sententia caret culpa. nam et in Graeco sono paenitentiae nomen non ex delicti confessione, sed ex animi demutatione compositum est, quam apud deum pro rerum uariantium sese occursu fieri ostendimus.
pass_a_gloss: And so you also misinterpret repentance with him, as if, indeed, because of instability or improvidence, or already from the remembrance of sin, he repents, since he said: 'I repent that I made Saul king', prescribing, of course, that repentance knows the confession of some evil work or error. Furthermore, not always. For it happens, indeed, even in good deeds, that there is a confession of repentance, to the envy and reproach of him who has been ungrateful for a benefit. Just as, also, then, around the person of Saul, who was to be burdened, it was announced by the Creator, who had not sinned, when he took Saul into the kingdom and increased him with the Holy Spirit; for he was still the best, as he said, 'There was not such a one among the sons of Israel' - he had chosen him most worthily. But nor had he been ignorant of how it would turn out. For no one will attribute improvidence to God, whom, not denying, you confess to be God and provident. For this, indeed, is a property of his divinity. But the evil deed of Saul, as I said, burdened his repentance with a profession, which, with no sin around the choosing of Saul, is a consequence that is rather to be understood as envious than criminal. Behold, you say, I notice it as criminal around the Ninevites, with the Scripture saying through Jonah: 'And the Lord repented of the evil which he had said he would do to them, and he did not do it.' Just as Jonah himself said to God: 'Therefore, I fled beforehand to Tarshish, because I knew you to be merciful and full of mercy, patient and very merciful, repenting of evils.' Therefore, it is well that he sent ahead the title of the best God, namely, the most patient over the evil and most abundant in mercy and pity over those acknowledging and lamenting their sins, such as the Ninevites then were. For if he is the best who is such, you ought to have desisted from this earlier, that evil does not pertain to such a one, that is, to the best. And since even Marcion defends the good tree as producing evil fruits, and yet he named evil, which the best does not comprehend, is there perhaps some interpretation underlying those evils to be understood, which can also have occurred in the best? There is, indeed. We say, finally, that evil is now signified not which is reduced to the nature of the Creator, as if evil, but which is to the power, as if of a judge; according to which he announced: 'I am he who creates evils', and: 'Behold, I send evils upon you', not sinful, but avenging. Of which we have sufficiently washed away the infamy as befitting a judge. Just as, however, although evils are said, they are not reprehended in a judge, nor do they show the judge to be evil by this name, so also this evil will be understood now, which is deputed from those judicial evils and pertains to the judge with them. For even among the Greeks, evils are sometimes put for vexations and injuries, not for malignities, just as in this passage. And so, if the Creator repented of his evil, as if of a creature, indeed, to be reproached and judged for sin, yet neither here will any admitted crime be reckoned to the Creator, who had deservedly and justly decreed the abolition of the most wicked city. Thus, what he had justly destined. Not destining evilly, from justice, not from evil, he had destined: but he named the punishment itself evil from the evil and merit of the passion. Therefore, you will say, if you excuse evil as a name of justice, because he had justly destined destruction for the Ninevites, so also he is to be blamed, who undoubtedly did not repent of justice, but repented. On the contrary, I say, God does not repent of justice, and it remains to acknowledge now what God's repentance is. For it is not, if a man repents from the remembrance of much sin, sometimes also from the ingratitude of some good work, therefore God also repents in the same way. Inasmuch as God neither admits evil nor condemns good, in so far is there no place for repentance of good or evil with him. For even this same Scripture determines for you, with Samuel saying to Saul: 'The Lord has torn the kingdom of Israel from your hand today and will give it to your neighbor, who is better than you, and Israel will be split into two parts, and it will not turn back, nor will it repent, because he is not a man to repent.' This definition, therefore, establishes a different form of divine repentance in all things, which is not reckoned from improvidence or levity or any condemnation of good or evil work, just like human repentance. What, therefore, will be the manner of divine repentance? It is now clear, if you do not refer it to human conditions. For nothing else is understood than a simple conversion of the prior sentence, which can also be admitted without reprehension, even in a man, much less in God, whose every sentence lacks fault. For even in the Greek sound, the name of repentance is composed not from the confession of sin, but from the change of mind, which we show to happen with God because of the occurrence of changing things.

can refer to punishment or vengeance

bible_refs.note: God's repentance over making Saul king

pass_b_english: You are misreading repentance in God's case, as if He repented out of instability or improvidence, or simply because He remembers some sin — since He said, 'I repent that I made Saul king,' as though repentance always means confessing an evil deed or mistake. But it does not always work that way. Scripture itself shows repentance confessed even over good deeds, to the envy and reproach of the one who proved ungrateful for a benefit. Take Saul: the Creator, who had not sinned, announced His repentance about burdening Saul when He took him into the kingdom and increased him with the Holy Spirit — for he was still the best, as God said, 'There was not such a one among the sons of Israel,' and He had chosen him most worthily. Yet He was not ignorant of how it would turn out. No one will saddle God with improvidence, since you yourself confess Him to be God and provident; providence is the very property of His divinity. The evil deed of Saul, as I said, burdened God's repentance with a profession that — with no sin attaching to the choice of Saul — is to be understood as envious rather than criminal. (1 Samuel 15:35)

You object: 'But I see it as criminal in the case of the Ninevites, for Jonah says: "The Lord repented of the evil which He had said He would do to them, and He did not do it." And Jonah himself said to God: "Therefore I fled beforehand to Tarshish, because I knew you to be merciful and full of mercy, patient and very merciful, repenting of evils."' Well put — he led with the title of the best God, the most patient over the wicked and most abundant in mercy and pity toward those who acknowledge and lament their sins, like the Ninevites then. If that is what 'best' means, you should have stopped earlier: evil does not belong to such a one, that is, to the best. Even Marcion admits a good tree cannot produce evil fruit, yet he named an evil that the best cannot comprehend. Is there some interpretation of those evils that could also have occurred in the best? There is. We say that 'evil' here does not mean evil reduced to the Creator's nature, but evil assigned to His power as Judge — according to which He announced: 'I am He who creates evils,' and: 'Behold, I send evils upon you' — not sinful, but avenging. We have sufficiently cleared the infamy of such evils as befitting a Judge. Just as evils are spoken of a judge without reproach, nor do they make the judge evil by that name, so this 'evil' is to be understood as drawn from judicial evils and belonging to the Judge. Even among the Greeks, 'evils' sometimes means vexations and injuries, not malignities — just as in this passage. So if the Creator repented of His 'evil' as if it were a creature to be reproached and judged for sin, yet no admitted crime will be reckoned to the Creator, who justly and deservedly decreed the abolition of the most wicked city. What He justly destined, He destined not evilly but from justice, not from evil; He named the punishment itself 'evil' from the evil and merit of its suffering. (Jonah 3:10)

So you will say: if you excuse 'evil' as a name of justice because He justly destined destruction for the Ninevites, then He is also to be blamed for repenting of justice, which is not to be repented of. On the contrary, God does not repent of justice. It remains to acknowledge what God's repentance actually is. It is not that because a man repents from the memory of much sin, sometimes even from the ingratitude of some good work, God repents in the same way. Inasmuch as God neither admits evil nor condemns good, to that extent there is no place for repentance of good or evil with Him. The same Scripture determines this for you, when Samuel says to Saul: 'The Lord has torn the kingdom of Israel from your hand today and will give it to your neighbor, who is better than you, and Israel will be split in two, and it will not turn back nor repent, because He is not a man to repent.' This definition establishes a different form of divine repentance in all things — not reckoned from improvidence or levity or any condemnation of good or evil work, like human repentance. What then is the manner of divine repentance? It is now clear, if you do not refer it to human conditions. Nothing else is understood than a simple conversion of the prior sentence, which can be admitted without reproach even in a man, much less in God, whose every sentence lacks fault. Even in the Greek, the word for repentance is composed not from confession of sin but from change of mind — which we show happens with God because of the occurrence of changing things.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex theological distinctions between 'malitia' as sin versus 'malitia' as judicial punishment. All scripture citations (1 Samuel 15:35, Jonah 3:10, and the Samuel/Saul passage) are correctly identified and matched to the Latin text. The distinction between human and divine repentance (metanoia/conversion of mind) is preserved.
